newsitem.title: UK: Unions say they to meet Ford chief this week.
newsitem.headline: Unions say they to meet Ford chief this week.

text.p: Leaders of the Transport and General Workers Union expect to hold talks this week with a senior Ford Motor Co official in an attempt to reverse planned British job cuts, a union spokesman said on Tuesday.

Andrew Murray of the T&GWU said union chiefs had been told by the company they would meet Jac Nasser, president of Ford Automotive Operations and Chairman of Ford Europe, on Thursday and Friday, probably in central London.
Ford spokesman Simon Sproule, however, denied that a date had been set for the meeting although he said it would be held quite soon. He said talk of meetings on Thursday and Friday was "speculation".
Last month, Ford offered the unions a chance to talk to Nasser about the 1,300 planned job cuts at the company's Halewood plant near Liverpool in northwestern England.
Unions decided then, after talks with Ford's British management, to ballot 30,000 car workers on whether to strike in protest at the job cuts. The process was expected to take up to six weeks.
Despite a noisy picket by Ford workers, the company refused to make any changes in the planned redundancies at Halewood.
Asked if union chiefs exected to persuade the company to change its mind about Halewood this week, Murray said: "We certainly hope so."

Unions say that mass meetings of British Ford workers last month produced overwhelming support for strike action in what they have called the most serious dispute in the motor industry for two decades.

The cuts at Halewood amount to about one job in every three at the plant where Ford plans to continue to build the current model Escort model until 2000 and then replace it with a new, Escort-based model.
Halewood workers said they were being targetted because employment legislation made it easier to dismiss them than workers at plants producing the Escort in Germany and Spain.

Britain's Observer newspaper said on Sunday that Ford might close its Transit van plant at Southampton on the south coast with the loss of 2,000 jobs. Production of a new Transit would be concentrated in Genk, Belgium.
Ford dismissed the report as speculative, while Murray said the unions did not plan to raise the matter with Nasser at this week's talks.
